analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the requirement that workers on federally funded construction be paid local prevailing wages.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate in April 2026 with 9 Republican sponsors and has not moved since it was referred to committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The Davis-Bacon Act requires companies working on federally funded construction to pay workers the wages that prevail locally for their trade — often union-level rates. This bill repeals those wage requirements 30 days after enactment, leaving existing contracts alone. If it became law, contractors could legally pay federal construction workers less, and any other law that references those wage rules would lose effect.
analysis.who_benefits: Construction firms and developers that bid on federal projects would save the most: the wage floor would disappear, letting them pay below the local prevailing rate and underbid rivals who pay full rates. Supporters of repeal argue taxpayers also gain if federal construction gets cheaper; that saving is debated, and it would come out of workers' paychecks.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Davis-Bacon wage requirements, ending the mandate that federal construction pay the local prevailing wage, effective 30 days after enactment.
Grandfathers contracts already in existence, and contracts made from bids already outstanding, at the 30-day mark — so the change hits future federal projects.

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federally funded projects — laborers, electricians, plumbers, and other trades — would likely see their pay fall where prevailing wages currently lift it above what contractors would otherwise pay. Communities that rely on those wage standards would also feel it as local wage norms weaken.
analysis.who_pays_short: Trades workers on federal construction jobs

drawbacks.text: The main cost falls on the workers themselves: the whole point of Davis-Bacon is to keep federal dollars from driving down area wages, so repeal removes that protection for trades workers.

Supporters argue in good faith that prevailing wage rules raise federal construction costs — historically by roughly 10% or more in some studies — and add compliance paperwork that burdens small contractors; repeal would end that. The tradeoff is that any savings to taxpayers come largely out of worker wages.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Contractors and taxpayers who value lower federal construction costs gain something real, but the core effect is a pay cut for a defined group of workers on federally funded projects. Because the bill repeals the wage floor entirely rather than reforming how it is administered, the burden lands squarely on workers and the benefit on the companies that employ them.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on April 30, 2026, read twice, and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it has sat without any further action.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Lee introduced the Davis-Bacon Repeal Act on April 30, 2026, joined by eight Republican cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; the action history shows no markup, vote, or floor action since.

The bill text repeals subchapter IV of chapter 31 of title 40 — the Davis-Bacon wage requirements — and voids any legal reference to them, 30 days after enactment, while sparing existing contracts and bids.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost: the bill is still parked in committee, and current prevailing wage requirements remain in force for federal construction.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — the bill is stalled in committee

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.role: U.S. Senator from Utah; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Davis-Bacon wage requirements and sought Republican cosponsors.

for.name: 8 of 53 Senate Republicans
for.role: Original cosponsors (Sens. Cruz, Scott of South Carolina, Johnson, Lankford, Britt, Budd, Ernst, Scott of Florida)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors of the repeal bill.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors are Republicans; no Democrat or Independent signed on, and the bill has not come to any vote.

industries.note: Repeal would let these firms pay below the local prevailing wage on federally funded projects, cutting their labor costs at the direct expense of the trades workers they hire.
Davis-Bacon prevailing wage rates typically track union-scale pay, so repeal would strip wage protections the unionized trades rely on and make lower-wage competitors more viable on federal jobs.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to the Senate HELP Committee without a hearing or markup — which is where this one has sat since April 2026 — almost never reach the floor, especially labor bills with no Democratic support. Unless the committee acts or the bill is attached to something larger, it is likely to die at the end of this Congress.
